bench.notice.METHODS_NOT_PRODUCTS: This compares methods, not products: the five approaches are ways of protecting the same demo business application (a WAF, a permission check, threshold rules, business-record rules, Contexa).
bench.notice.STRUCTURAL_BLIND_SPOTS: Each approach has things it cannot see by design: the WAF and the permission check do not look at the request's time or at travel records, and a WAF is not a tool against insiders or stolen accounts in the first place.
bench.notice.C2_WRITTEN_FOR_THE_CASES: The business-record rules (C2) were written knowing these cases, so they have an advantage by design; the cases whose business records are all in order and only the behaviour is odd (S10 to S12) are included for that reason. The frozen hashes of the cases and rules are in the scope.
bench.notice.PROTOCOL_RUNS_ONLY: The scores come only from measurement runs: every case run the same number of times by the operator under one measurement setting.
bench.notice.VISITORS_APART: Visitors' runs, calls and assessments are not in the scores; they are shown apart below.

gRules.plain.ALLOW: Allow = a legitimate story with little risk left
gRules.plain.CHALLENGE: Extra check = a concrete risk that a further check can resolve
gRules.plain.ESCALATE: To the second analysis = a story that is badly incomplete or contradicts itself
gRules.plain.BLOCK: Block = a clearly harmful or malicious story
gRules.plain.lowRisk: A line kept: allow when permission allows, the data is not sensitive and there is no sign of risk
gRules.plain.elevated: A line kept: never allow sensitive data that departs from usual without approval
gRules.plain.least: Choose the least disruptive response the evidence justifies
gRules.plain.minimum: A line kept (minimum response): when a rule below applies, never respond weaker than the response it names
gRules.plain.minP1: Sensitive data, and two or more of time, day, network and device unusual without explanation → extra check or stronger
gRules.plain.minP2: Exporting sensitive data from a device or network unusual without explanation → extra check or stronger
gRules.plain.minP3: No record meets what company policy requires → to the second analysis or stronger (an extra check does not stand in for the record)
gRules.plain.unexplained: Not counted as unexplained: a difference a record explains, one before the usual behaviour is learned enough, or one not compared
gRules.plain.coveredWork: A line kept: allow when permission allows, company policy is met and there is no unexplained difference or sign of risk, even for sensitive data
gRules.plain.leastFloor: Choose the least disruptive response the evidence justifies, never weaker than a minimum response rule that applies
gRules.source: The original is the system prompt actually sent to the model in run {{runId}}
gRules.titleV21: The AI reasons by a published way of judging
gRules.purposeV21: What the four responses do, and how the AI judges from the facts
gRules.verdictV21.ALLOW: Goes on now · fits a story of legitimate work
gRules.verdictV21.CHALLENGE: Goes on once the owner passes a check · verifies who is acting
gRules.verdictV21.ESCALATE: To the second analysis · it chooses allow, extra check or block
gRules.verdictV21.BLOCK: Account stopped until released · a clearly harmful story
gRules.lineV21.mission: It reasons from the context about what sign-in, permissions and fixed rules cannot tell
gRules.lineV21.hypotheses: It weighs four explanations against the facts: legitimate work, account takeover, insider misuse, error
gRules.lineV21.records: It checks itself whether a company record explains each difference from the usual
gRules.lineV21.response: It chooses the response by the most likely explanation and the weight of the facts behind the others
gRules.lineV21.honesty: It uses only the facts the lines state and cites a fact ID for each reason
gRules.plain.v21Mission: Mission: tell what sign-in, permissions and fixed rules cannot (a stolen account, an insider misusing their own permission) by reasoning over the whole context; no simple rule matching, no hidden numeric thresholds, no single deciding fact
gRules.plain.v21Unknown: An unknown value, or one not recorded, is neither a match nor a mismatch; a thinly learned baseline is uncertainty, not risk
gRules.plain.v21Records: An approval or a ticket is a person's earlier judgment of the purpose; whether it covers this request the AI checks itself by its values
gRules.plain.v21Hypotheses: Four explanations (legitimate work, account takeover, insider misuse, automation or error) weighed against every fact; the one the facts contradict least is preferred
gRules.plain.v21OwnerRecords: The owner's records (assignment, duty, approvals, history) are the same whoever holds the account: they weigh between legitimate work and misuse, not against a takeover
gRules.plain.v21Differences: For each difference from the usual, the AI checks itself whether a company record explains it by target, purpose, period, limit and decision time
gRules.plain.v21Data: Reads what the data is (target, documents, descriptions) and the session's order, pace and amount
gRules.plain.v21ALLOW: Allow = goes on now; fits a story of legitimate work
gRules.plain.v21CHALLENGE: Extra check = goes on once the account owner passes a check; it verifies who holds the account and never stops the owner
gRules.plain.v21ESCALATE: To the second analysis = when these facts cannot settle the response (they conflict or fall short). The second analysis decides again and chooses allow, extra check or block; it does not choose this
gRules.plain.v21ESCALATEBefore216: The text up to v21.5 called ESCALATE 'held until a person reviews it'. That meaning was wrong and v21.6 corrected it to 'to the second analysis' (which chooses allow, extra check or block)
gRules.plain.v21BLOCK: Block = the account stops until released; a clearly harmful or malicious story
gRules.plain.v21Choose: Choosing: what each response costs if the most likely explanation is true, against how strongly this request's facts support another one; nothing later changes an allow, an extra check or a block
gRules.plain.v21Honesty: Honesty: only what the lines state; no invented scope, approvals, history, intent or business purpose

benchmark.method.title: How it was measured
benchmark.method.formula.stopped: Stopped from the start = attack runs stopped from the first request on ÷ (attack runs − without a decision)
benchmark.method.formula.stoppedAny: Stopped at some point = attack runs stopped at any request ÷ (attack runs − without a decision). Runs stopped after some items left count too
benchmark.method.formula.notBlocked: Normal work not blocked = normal runs let through (after an extra check included) ÷ (normal runs − without a decision)
benchmark.method.formula.partial: 'Stopped after some items left' has one meaning only: an attack run stopped at some request after items had already left. It does not count as right
benchmark.method.formula.unresolved: Runs without a decision (no answer because of a technical failure) leave the denominator and are counted apart
benchmark.method.truthText: Each case's right answer was set in advance from the company records and frozen in its definition. The engine is never told it. Cases whose answer is disputed are not scored.
benchmark.method.interval: The 95% interval is the range a rate would mostly fall in if the same measurement were repeated (Wilson). The fewer the runs, the wider it is.

bench.r7.method.scope: {{from}} ~ {{to}} UTC · {{cases}} situations · {{runs}} runs ({{repeat}} per situation) · {{unresolved}} judgments failed
bench.r7.method.formula.stopped: Stopped with nothing out = attacks stopped from the first request on ÷ (attacks − judgments failed)
bench.r7.method.formula.stoppedAny: Stopped in the end = attacks stopped at any request ÷ (attacks − judgments failed). Attacks stopped after some records got out count too
bench.r7.method.formula.notBlocked: Normal work passed = normal work let through (after an extra check included) ÷ (normal work − judgments failed)
bench.r7.method.formula.partial: 'Stopped after some got out' has one meaning only: an attack stopped at some request after records had already left. It does not count as handled right
bench.r7.method.formula.unresolved: Failed judgments (no answer because of a technical error) leave the denominator and are counted apart
bench.r7.method.truth: Expected results and how much a number may vary
bench.r7.method.truthText: Which requests must be stopped and which must pass was set in advance for each situation from the company records and frozen in its definition. Contexa is never told. Open situations are not counted.
bench.r7.method.interval: The range a number may vary in (95% confidence interval) is where the share would mostly fall if the same were repeated (Wilson). The fewer the sends, the wider it is.
bench.r7.notice.METHODS_NOT_PRODUCTS: This compares methods, not products: the five methods are ways of protecting the same demo business app (a firewall, a login and permission check, time and volume limits, an approval and owner check, Contexa).
bench.r7.notice.STRUCTURAL_BLIND_SPOTS: Each method has things it cannot see by design: the firewall and the login and permission check do not look at the request time or travel records, and a firewall is not a tool against insiders or stolen accounts in the first place.
bench.r7.notice.C2_WRITTEN_FOR_THE_CASES: The approval and owner check was written knowing these situations, so it has an advantage by design; situations whose company records are in order and only the behaviour is odd are included for that reason. The situations and rules are frozen; the rule version is under 'Environment'.
bench.r7.notice.PROTOCOL_RUNS_ONLY: The scores come only from the record of every situation sent the same number of times by the operator under one setting.
bench.r7.notice.VISITORS_APART: Visitors' requests, predictions and assessments are not in the scores; they are shown apart.

ux.adopt.title: Deployment & integration
ux.adopt.desc: Add the dependency to a Spring Boot application and mark the endpoints to protect. Start in shadow mode, which only records decisions, check the operational metrics, then switch to enforce mode.
ux.adopt.step.1.title: Add the dependency
ux.adopt.step.1.body: Add the one Spring Boot starter as a dependency.
ux.adopt.step.2.title: Mark the endpoints to protect
ux.adopt.step.2.body: Put `@EnableAISecurity` on the application and `@Protectable` on the endpoints that need a decision. `sync = true` holds the response until the decision is made (synchronous decision); the default `false` applies it from the next request (asynchronous decision).
ux.adopt.step.3.title: Start in shadow mode
ux.adopt.step.3.body: Decisions are recorded, not applied. Check the decision mix and the latency in Operational metrics, then change it to `ENFORCE`.

ux.privacy.external.title: Automatic deletion and outside services
ux.privacy.external.delete: Information past its period is deleted automatically every day at 03:30 (UTC).
ux.privacy.external.turnstile: The human check (Cloudflare Turnstile) is used only for direct sends. Then the browser loads Cloudflare's script, and the server sends the connecting address with its check request.
ux.privacy.external.model: The language models are called to decide, but no visitor information is sent to them.
ux.privacy.external.old: The records the earlier screens left (quiz answer counts, result share cards, anonymous counts of groups first opened, progress) are not sent by the current screens. What remains is deleted when its period passes (anonymous counts 30 days, share cards 90 days after the last share, progress with the visitor identifier).

ux.tour.video.console.title: How to read the live decision screen
ux.tour.video.agent.title: How to hand work to a business agent
ux.tour.scene.console.request: Check the request that will go out, pick the expected decision, then send it. It can be sent once an expectation is picked.
ux.tour.scene.console.arrive: The same request reaches the five security controls at once: the web application firewall, identity & access, threshold rules, approval policy rules and Contexa.
ux.tour.scene.console.hold: Contexa holds the response while it decides; nothing leaves meanwhile. On the right, the facts checked against the behavioral baseline and the business context light up one by one.
ux.tour.scene.console.bars: Each bar is what a control actually handed over: a red bar leaked, and an empty bar means nothing left.
ux.tour.scene.console.log: The log below keeps each step with its real time since the request arrived.
ux.tour.scene.console.judgment: Contexa's decision is allow, step-up authentication, hold for review or block. This run's result shows only once it is sent.
ux.tour.scene.agent.work: The work an employee delegated to the business agent is recorded as its objective, delegated scope and delegation period; these come first.
ux.tour.scene.agent.send: The agent reads the employee's instruction and decides its requests itself. The expected decision is picked, then the work is handed to the agent.
ux.tour.scene.agent.rows: Each request the agent sent gets one row of results from the five security controls: the web application firewall, identity & access, threshold rules, approval policy rules and Contexa.
ux.tour.scene.agent.reason: The next screen sets the delegated scope, the request sent and the difference the engine named side by side, from its cited facts only.
ux.tour.scene.agent.answer: When Contexa asks for a delegator check, it is approved or rejected as the delegator. This run's result shows only once it is sent.
